claims.text: The baseline non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy is a single-phase hexagonal material with a first-order magnetostructural transition near room temperature.
Conventionally processed FeMnNiGeSi exhibits a sharp, hysteretic magnetostructural transition with a high peak magnetic entropy change.
The conventionally processed baseline has relatively coarse grains and a lower surface-to-volume ratio.
Rapid solidification by melt-spinning, possibly followed by a brief anneal, will produce nanostructured FeMnNiGeSi ribbons.
The melt-spun state will have refined grains and a higher grain-boundary density.
Melt-spun ribbons will have a higher surface-to-volume ratio than the bulk baseline.
The increased grain-boundary density provides additional nucleation sites for the first-order magnetostructural transformation.
Additional grain-boundary nucleation sites make the magnetostructural transformation more uniform and gradual.
Nanostructuring spreads the transformation over a wider temperature and magnetic-field interval.
Reduced domain size and increased grain-boundary area diminish energy barriers associated with domain-wall motion.
Lower domain-wall-motion barriers and a more gradual transition reduce magnetic hysteresis during low-field cycling.
Nanostructured ribbons will display a broader but slightly lower peak magnetic entropy change than the baseline.
The hysteresis reduction will occur without completely sacrificing the amplitude of the magnetic entropy change.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of the ribbons will increase heat-exchange rates.
Faster heat exchange and reduced hysteresis are beneficial characteristics for magnetic-refrigeration performance.
The predicted effects are limited to compositions retaining a single-phase hexagonal structure and a first-order magnetostructural transition near the operating temperature under low applied fields.

contradictions.description: The baseline is variously defined as an arc-melted or conventionally processed sample and as possibly a melt-spun microribbon, while melt-spinning is also the proposed intervention. If the baseline is already melt-spun, the intervention does not cleanly distinguish the proposed processing effect.

The anneal is described as possible or optional in the hypothesis and intervention, but the falsification experiment specifies that the rapidly solidified samples are followed by a defined brief anneal. This changes the intervention and prevents unambiguous attribution to melt-spinning versus annealing.

The initial state is called 'as-deposited' while also being described as arc-melted or conventionally processed; these are not necessarily deposition states, making the starting condition internally ambiguous.
